articles.title: Former Seattle City Council president launches AI-powered site to track and report on City Hall
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Sara Nelson, the former Seattle City Council president, is making her debut as a publisher and commentator, with an eye toward boosting civic engagement, and a little help from AI agents.

CivicTide, which Nelson launched Monday at civictide.org , tracks and reports on Seattle City Council legislation from introduction to final vote. Policy briefs — such as this one on Councilmember Dan Strauss’ plan to create RV parking permits for people living in vehicles — summarize what a bill would do, explain the stakes, and juxtapose the “spin” from backers against the site’s analysis.

Readers can use built-in tools on the site to quickly email councilmembers on specific issues or post their views on social media. CivicTide arrives one day before the council starts its budget deliberations, which Nelson said was deliberate timing.
“I’m trying to solve for the hassle of civic engagement,” Nelson said in an interview with GeekWire, describing it as an effort to help create “more accountable, accessible governance.”

Each policy brief links to the underlying ordinance and committee records. The site also aggregates and links to coverage elsewhere, and publishes opinion pieces on specific issues, such as this one calling Mayor Katie Wilson’s freeze on police hiring bonuses “downright reckless.”

Does that make CivicTide partisan? “Every piece of media, even the reporting pages, everything has a slant,” Nelson said. At the same time, she said she will aim for neutrality in describing what a bill would do, while confining her own read to the “spin vs. reality” section.
Asked whether she would be open to Mayor Wilson writing a guest column for CivicTide, Nelson didn’t hesitate. “I would welcome that,” she said.

How it works: Behind the scenes of the website, a custom AI-powered content management system ingests city legislative data hourly and gives Nelson a ranked queue of what’s worth writing about. It offers draft posts ready for her to review, edit, and rework as needed before publication.

It was built by Viet Nguyen , a veteran Seattle tech communications executive who has developed a specialty in building political and civic websites. He used AI to write the whole thing from scratch, including the public site, the backend, and the editorial workflow he calls the newsroom.

Nelson acknowledged that using AI this way could raise questions among the press and general public, and said she expects to be asked about it. “My motto is, don’t get left behind,” she said. “We have to use every tool within our toolbox to actually make government more accessible.”
She approves everything the system produces: “There is always a human behind the machinery.”

Changing media landscape: The site also aggregates and links to stories from established local outlets, chosen for their connection to active legislation, from a set flagged by the AI in the backend for Nelson’s editorial consideration.

As in many media markets, Seattle has a smaller set of reporters covering City Hall than it used to. Nelson said people tend to get their information about City Hall from limited sources, and the goal is to help round out the conversation and sources of news.

For example, in addition to the Seattle Times, the site’s “In the press” section currently links to KUOW, KING 5, KOMO News, The Seattle Medium, and a post from the personal blog of Tim Burgess, the former City Council president who served as deputy mayor under Bruce Harrell.
Articles from The Stranger, Publicola, GeekWire and many other sites are among the sources served up for Nelson’s consideration in the CivicTide backend.
Meanwhile, AI has made these kinds of sites cheaper and easier to build.

GeekWire profiled a similar project in April: Next30Days , built by former Amazon product manager Julien Clayton, which pulls agendas from the same Legistar system and summarizes them to get people to attend meetings. It takes no position on the bills it covers.

Background and perspective: Nelson, who co-founded Fremont Brewing, spent four years on the council, two as its president, and was its most consistently business-friendly member, advocating for police hiring, addiction treatment and permitting changes.
She lost her seat in November to Dionne Foster and left office in January. Asked whether she plans to run for council again, and whether CivicTide is part of that, Nelson said no.
Support from business leaders: CivicTide is debuting at a time when business leaders and elected officials from outside Seattle are becoming more vocal about the city’s economic direction.

The site’s launch announcement includes testimonials from business and neighborhood leaders, including chef Ethan Stowell, SODO Business Improvement Area executive director Erin Goodman, Joyale Seafood owner Vincent Zhao, Gary Lee of the Chinatown-International District Public Safety Council, and Tina Bueche, a former president of the Pioneer Square Community Council.

In the announcement, Stowell said the restaurant industry “feels totally unrepresented in City Hall,” and that small businesses lack the time and staff to keep up with the city’s shifting proposals even though they absorb the consequences. He said CivicTide would let them track the legislation that affects them and weigh in “before it’s a done deal.”

Nonprofit status: The publisher of CivicTide is SeaFor, a 501(c)(4) social welfare nonprofit that Nelson runs, registered in Washington state. Donors to a 501(c)(4) aren’t required to be disclosed publicly in the state, and Nelson declined to name hers in the interview with GeekWire last week.

The organization does plan to contribute to an independent expenditure campaign in the District 5 race, the only council seat on the ballot this year, Nelson said. If SeaFor is among that campaign’s largest donors, its own top three contributors will be named on the mailers.
Nelson said she’s supporting Julie Kang in that race, though a formal endorsement would follow interviews with Kang and Nilu Jenks, scored against a rubric.

GeekWire profiled Nguyen in August . His recent projects include Culliton2026.org , an AI-generated guide to how state Supreme Court candidates might rule on Washington’s new millionaires’ tax. That site took a few hours and about $100 in AI tokens.

CivicTide is a bigger undertaking. Nelson said her organization’s budget is $163,000 for July through December, with $55,000 to $65,000 of that going to site development and ongoing AI tokens. The rest covers legal costs and the planned independent expenditure, she said. She isn’t paying herself.

SeaFor’s other stated purpose is recruiting and supporting candidates whom Nelson calls pragmatic — a term she defined loosely, covering everyone from a small-business owner to “a neighbor on Aurora who’s sick of seeing the mayhem every Saturday night.”

articles.title: Ex-Zillow VP’s startup Truelist acquired by Mainstay in $18M expansion of real estate AI
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle-based real estate tech startup Truelist has been acquired by San Francisco-based Mainstay as part of an $18 million growth funding round aimed at expanding AI-powered tools across the residential property market.
Founded in 2024, Truelist built an AI-powered listing platform to help real estate brokers and agents manage, create, and distribute property listings across fragmented MLS systems.

Mainstay — which was carved out of Opendoor as an independent startup in August 2024 — operates an “intelligent system of record” that automates data and transactions across the residential real estate lifecycle, primarily serving major institutional investors.
Truelist founder and CEO Carey Armstrong brings a deep Seattle real estate tech background to Mainstay, where she will serve as chief strategy officer.

Armstrong spent seven years as vice president of Premier Agent at Zillow before co-founding real estate fintech Tomo in 2020, alongside former Zillow leader Greg Schwartz. That startup raised a $40 million seed round backed by high-profile investors, including former Trulia CEO Pete Flint and ex-Zillow chief executive Spencer Rascoff. Armstrong served as COO before launching Truelist four years later.

“I’m grateful to everyone who supported Truelist along the way, and especially to the team who put so much talent, care, and hard work into building,” Armstrong said on LinkedIn . “If you don’t know Mainstay yet, don’t worry, you will soon.”
For Mainstay, the deal allows the startup to expand beyond its core client base of large institutional investors into the broader market of brokerages, agents, and smaller property owners.

Mainstay is led by CEO Dod Fraser — the former president of Opendoor — alongside fellow Opendoor veterans J.D. Rasmussen and Michael Dulfer. The company’s new $18 million funding round was backed by investors including Khosla Ventures, Era Ventures, Parker89, Stackpoint, Alpaca VC, and FJ Labs.

Mainstay said it has facilitated more than $12 billion in real estate transactions and serves 95% of the 60 largest residential real estate investors. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

“Joining forces means we stop duplicating effort and start compounding it,” Armstrong said in a statement. “I have enormous respect for what Dod and the team have built, and I’m excited about what we can do together.”

articles.title: Seattle startups DexCare and Mila Health combine to expand AI patient scheduling
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle health-tech startup DexCare today announced it’s acquiring Mila Health, a fellow Seattle-area company that has built AI agents to call and text patients seeking medical appointments.
The startups did not disclose the terms of the deal.

DexCare, which spun out of Providence’s digital innovation group a decade ago, helps healthcare organizations fill appointment slots and manages information including patient referral requirements, insurance and scheduling protocols. The company serves 57 million patients nationwide, and customers include Kaiser Permanente, Piedmont, Texas Health Resources and Tampa General.

Mila’s technology can help answer questions related to available appointments and patient qualifications. The startup said it takes only hours to embed its technology into existing systems and launch AI agents.

“Healthcare can’t rely on out-of-the-box large language models because they’re unpredictable and can’t be audited,” said Shailu Verma, co-founder and CEO of Mila, in a statement. “With DexCare, providers and payers can configure an AI agent to complete the tasks they can’t staff for.”

Added Matt Blosl, CEO of DexCare: “AI solutions are everywhere, but health systems quickly realize that building the infrastructure, scaling the pilot, and managing the agent’s boundaries is untenable.”

Providence initially started DexCare to help with digital patient acquisition by better coordinating health system capacity and appointment booking. The startup has raised $146 million , with its most recent round totaling $75 million in 2023. It previously acquired Womp, a Bellingham, Wash.-based online commerce platform, in 2022.

The company was also a finalist for Health Innovation of the Year at the 2023 GeekWire Awards. It’s No. 43 on the GeekWire 200 , a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups, and has approximately 133 employees, according to PitchBook.

Verma helped launch Mila in January 2024 and previously served as chief product officer of strategy and innovation at UnitedHealth Group. He spent five years at Amazon Web Services as a product manager, leaving in 2021.

PitchBook reports that Mila participated in the Advanced Technology Development Center accelerator and that no equity or funding was exchanged as part of the program. The startup appears not to have raised any venture capital and has 25 employees.

articles.title: Plug and Play Seattle picks 11 startups for 4th cohort, from space robotics to biotech
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Plug and Play Seattle selected 11 startups for the fourth batch of its accelerator program, bringing together a group of founders building everything from space-servicing robotic arms and data-center optical links to opioid-countering antibody therapeutics.

The 12-week program kicks off today and runs through mid-December. Ten of the participating startups are based in Seattle, joined by Tokyo-based wireless power developer Aeterlink, which is participating in an exploratory international track to support its expansion into the U.S. and Pacific Northwest.

Programming will mix virtual sessions with in-person work across Plug and Play Seattle’s regional hubs at the University of Washington’s CoMotion Labs and the SNBL Global Gateway in Everett, Wash. The cohort will present their progress to investors and corporate partners at a Dec. 3 expo at the Boeing Future of Flight in Mukilteo.

“Seattle has the talent and research depth to build companies that shape entire industries,” said Jack Callaghan, director of Plug and Play Seattle, in a statement. “This cohort reflects that potential, from advancing drug discovery to building the infrastructure behind AI.”
Silicon Valley-based Plug and Play launched its Seattle presence in March 2025.

In addition to startup accelerators, Plug and Play runs corporate innovation programs and has an in-house venture capital fund that has backed companies such as including Dropbox, Guardant Health, Honey, Lending Club, N26, PayPal, and Rappi.

articles.title: Amazon blocks Meta’s Muse AI assistant in new standoff over agentic shopping
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon says it has cut off Meta’s new Muse personal AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com on behalf of customers, after attempting unsuccessfully to get the Facebook parent company to voluntarily exclude the e-commerce site from the experience.

The problem, Amazon says, is that it never agreed to any of it. Meta didn’t tell Amazon that Muse would access its store, the agent doesn’t identify itself when it browses, and it appears to capture and store customer credentials, which the company says could create privacy and security risks.

As of Sunday night, people trying to use Muse to shop on Amazon were seeing the popup, “Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.”

“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement.
Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday night.

The company said previously that Muse “has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods,” and that credentials a user shares “go into secure storage, so Muse can use them without seeing them, including passwords a person types into the browser themselves.”

Business partners: The standoff between the tech giants is especially notable because the two companies work together: Amazon products have been purchasable inside Facebook and Instagram since 2023, and Meta signed a multibillion-dollar deal in April to run agentic AI workloads on Amazon’s Graviton chips.
It’s part of a larger debate over who controls the online shopping experience and the customer relationship when AI agents buy items on behalf of consumers.
Amazon has spent the past year trying to keep outside agents off its site, suing Perplexity over its Comet browser and moving to block shopping agents from Google and OpenAI .
On Sunday night, Amazon said it is in direct conversation with Meta about the issue. Asked whether it would consider taking legal action, the company declined to comment.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. In addition to operating its flagship e-commerce site, Amazon generated more than $68 billion in ad revenue last year — a business that depends on people browsing its pages and seeing sponsored products.

Security implications: Muse can reach account pages and order history if a customer prompts it to do so, Amazon says. Because the agent doesn’t identify itself, the company says, that amounts to an undisclosed third party moving through customer accounts, processing transactions and handling sensitive data without Amazon’s knowledge or consent.

Amazon said agents that operate openly help keep the customer experience safe and reliable, and that other services buying on a customer’s behalf typically do so with the merchant’s agreement. It cited food delivery apps and the restaurants they take orders for, and online travel agencies and the airlines they book tickets with.
“Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience,” Amazon’s spokesperson said in the statement.

Legal maneuvering: Amazon won a preliminary injunction against Perplexity in March , then lost it on Aug. 4 , when the Ninth Circuit ruled that the user — not the AI company — was the one accessing Amazon’s computers under federal anti-hacking law.

The court denied Amazon’s petition for rehearing on Sept. 10. However, the ruling left one avenue open for Amazon: claims built on contracts and terms of service. The message Muse users are now seeing doesn’t accuse anyone of hacking but cites Amazon’s Conditions of Use.

How Muse works: Meta launched Muse on Sept. 8 as a personal agent that carries out multi-step tasks rather than answering one-off questions, connecting to services including email, calendar, payments, dining and shopping.
It’s free, with paid subscription tiers, and available on iOS, Android, muse.ai and WhatsApp.

Meta says the agent runs on a secure virtual machine , with its own browser, and checks with the user before sensitive actions like sending an email or making a purchase. A separate monitoring agent called Sentinel has to approve anything Muse sends to the internet.

The Muse launch materials describe the mechanism now at the center of the dispute: If a service has a public API, Muse can connect to it using credentials the user provides. If it has no API at all, Meta says, the agent “can use the service through a browser the way you would.”

Muse has caught on fast. A week after launch, it became the No. 1 free app in Apple’s U.S. App Store , ahead of ChatGPT. Early users have described it switching an auto insurance policy, hunting down discount codes at checkout, and loading an online grocery cart.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, an AI agent that researches products and makes recommendations. Its own agentic shopping feature, Buy for Me , finds items on external brands’ sites, but the company points out that Buy for Me identifies itself and lets brands opt out.

articles.title: After modern split, Capitol Hill corner home to old-time Canterbury Tavern readied for MOOV movement and fitness studio
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill has changed. The corner where the Canterbury Tavern soothed souls and damaged livers for decades will soon be providing curated low-impact wellness synergy.
Seattle boutique fitness studio MOOV is working on a major Capitol Hill expansion, with plans to open a new studio inside the historic Fredonia building at 15th Ave E and E Mercer.
The move will bring the brand’s community-centered fitness concept to the ground floor formerly occupied by the legendary Canterbury Ale House, according to permit paperwork filed with the city.

The nearly 120-year-old building, acquired in 2023 by Pacific Northwest commercial real estate investment and development firm Meriwether Partners as affordable provider Community Roots Housing sold off some of its long-held portfolio, has been undergoing a street level overhaul dividing the cavernous 5,000-square-foot former tavern and a short-lived restaurant that followed into two commercial suites. While building ownership initially envisioned food and beverage concepts, the split paved the way for another type of complementary business. Perhaps a future commercial neighbor will continue the Canterbury’s more hedonistic legacy.

15th Ave E’s current era of growth has been on pause as the old QFC block awaits a six-story redevelopment stalled along with major development across most of the Hill by high interest rates, inflation, and a suboptimal rental economy. In the meantime, arts groups like LOVECITYLOVE and the Punk Rock Flea Market are keeping the area busy . And small businesses like Sweet Mary’s Cherries are making temporary homes in the someday to be demolished buildings.

MOOV is making a more permanent investment with a planned $600,000 buildout of its new Fredonia space. It will come in a recent wave of major gym and fitness investments across Capitol Hill including the expansion of Henry’s Gymnasium with a 2024 opening on Boylston Ave and the plans for new gyms from Rain City Fit including its $10.1 million acquisition this year of 13th Ave’s old Auto Accessories building.

Commercial retail space at the Fredonia is listed at a base rent of $40.00 per square foot annually under a triple net structure including taxes, insurance, and upkeep. For the 1,752-square-foot street commercial suite adjacent to the future MOOV, base rent calculates to roughly $70,080 per year with the tenant also responsible for their proportionate share of property taxes, building insurance, and maintenance.

Founded in 2021 by Erin Dickieson , MOOV has built a loyal Seattle following across its Elliott Avenue mat and recovery sanctuary and its South Lake Union studio — a dedicated hub for the Lagree Method, where clients perform high-intensity, low-impact workouts using the spring-loaded Megaformer apparatus.

A 15th Ave E location marks the brand’s first venture onto Capitol Hill, bringing high-intensity, low-impact training, recovery amenities, and its dog-friendly, body-neutral community ethos to the changing street and marking a new start for the storied corner.
MOOV Capitol Hill will be located at 534 15th Ave E. Learn more at moovseattle.com .

articles.title: Seattle considers commercial lease transparency ordinance
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The lease listing for one of Capitol HIll’s more unusual commercial spaces
Prospective new Capitol Hill businesses could have an easier time securing a fair lease under new legislation under consideration by the Seattle City Council .

Proposed by the Office of Economic Development and sponsored by Human Services, Labor, and Economic Development Committee chair Alexis Mercedes Rinck , the commercial lease transparency ordinance requires landlords to disclose critical property data before tenants sign agreements.

For dense, historic commercial corridors like Capitol Hill where restaurants, bars, and retailers frequently lease older spaces with aging infrastructure, the measure would introduce new transparency rules for lease agreements.

Under the bill, landlords must provide tenants a signed copy of the lease at execution, an additional copy on request, and the most recent Certificate of Occupancy on file with the city. Landlords must also attach a disclosure form detailing known infrastructure and utility conditions, and share previous-year records alongside first-year estimates for shared building operating fees, commonly known as triple-net expenses. Tenants charged these fees gain the right to inspect actual operating invoices annually.
OED officials reported that hidden infrastructure defects and unpredictable fee spikes disproportionately burden minority- and immigrant-owned enterprises.
The rules exempt residential units, offices, research laboratories, and medical facilities.

A council analysis highlighted several challenges, noting that enforcement depends on individual tenants filing civil lawsuits to prove financial injury, as city agencies will not issue citations for these disclosure rules. Analysts also noted that older occupancy certificates do not guarantee land-use approval for a new business concept, and smaller property owners may struggle with the administrative workload.
OED says the proposed policy was formed after providing technical assistance and reviewing leases for hundreds of small businesses navigating commercial disputes and tenant improvements.
If passed, the transparency rules would be in effect for leases executed after July 1, 2027.
Council action is slated for this fall with a final vote aimed for October 20th.

articles.title: Mayor orders revamp of Seattle emergency management and alert protocols
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: At this summer’s Urban Survival Fair in Volunteer Park

Following the controversy around the city’s response following the deadly Seattle Center shootout, Mayor Katie Wilson has signed an executive order to overhaul the city’s emergency response and disaster planning.

According to city officials, the directive addresses gaps identified in an independent 2025 assessment, operational reviews from the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and lessons learned from the Bite of Seattle festival shooting. Wilson said “the old way of doing things is no longer enough” to protect the public from modern hazards and serious incidents in her administration’s announcement .

The order directs city departments to establish a unified strategy, standardize internal operations, and expand community preparedness. Under the directive, the Seattle Office of Emergency Management will guide all municipal departments to define their operational roles and create plans by late 2027 to ensure public services continue during disasters.

The Wilson administration order establishes an interdepartmental team to institute mandatory employee disaster training, conduct regular multi-agency drills, and establish clear operational standards for who can send public warnings through the AlertSeattle notification network.

Community efforts beyond City Hall will also help the city be resilient in the face of emergencies and disasters. CHS reported here on the efforts of the North Capitol Hill Emergency Hub to provide education and resources.

At the neighborhood level, the Mayor’s Office said the city will partner with local agencies to integrate safety education into public schools, develop localized disaster plans, and install waterfront tsunami warning signs.

articles.title: Wilson Seeks to Clean House Ahead of First Budget Rollout
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: On Friday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson signed an executive order intended to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the City’s operations while fostering the sustainability of its budget.

The executive order calls for the establishment of a cross-departmental work group that will work to strengthen the City’s operations and improve both the effectiveness and efficiency of the services it provides. The interdepartmental team is charged with delivering a set of recommendations of how to accomplish this by March 30th of next year.

The list of possible topics for the team to discuss includes outcome-based budget evaluations, ways to streamline and track capital projects, implementing modern technology and money management practices, practicing risk management, and improving the City’s customer service.
“We live in a time right now where trust in government and institutions generally is very, very low,” Wilson said. “So, I believe that we really need to show that we can deliver.”

City Finance Director Dwight Dively, who held the position of Finance Director for the City for more than a decade before leaving for a 16-year stint as the director of King County's Office of Performance, Strategy and Budget, returned to work for the City earlier this year. Dively didn’t mince words about what he found upon his return.

"I left a city government that ran well," Dively said in a press release. "Coming back, I was struck by how much had changed, and not for the better. There is real work to do here, and I am glad to be part of doing it. Seattle residents trust us with their money and their services. Being a responsible steward of that trust is the job."

When The Urbanist asked for examples of current inefficiencies, Dively shared that right now, each City department has their own travel system, instead of utilizing a city-wide system that could both provide organizational discounts and more accountability. Another example mentioned was a lack of uniformity in the City trying to collect payments from insurance when a member of the public damages a City vehicle. Dively said that King County increased revenue more than $1 million per year through this practice.

City Budget Office Director Aly Pennucci offered another example, saying that some community service providers have contracts with multiple City departments. Having one streamlined contract per service provider would be more efficient for everyone.

Part of the work called for in the executive order will be ensuring the City has the right systems and technologies in place to optimize for efficiencies, whether that’s improving the experience of using the Find It, Fix It app, updating accounting rules, or making sure the Seattle Police Department is effectively tracking its officers’ overtime.

Dively told The Urbanist that the City doesn’t currently have an enterprise risk management program, which involves identifying the biggest risks in each department in order to manage those risks more effectively.
“In my opinion, we could save millions, if not tens of millions, of dollars every year, if we did [risk management] effectively,” Dively said.

A structural deficit has loomed over the City for the past several years, with the Jumpstart payroll tax acting as the primary means of closing the gap on a year-by-year basis. The estimated deficit for 2027 stood at $175 million .

However, as part of beginning the work to improve city governance, Wilson said that her new proposed budget being released on Tuesday doesn’t have a projected deficit in either the general fund or the Jumpstart fund through 2030.

“Coming into the Mayor's Office, I was very aware that we were facing a structural deficit and that we could not keep lurching from shortfall to shortfall, year after year,” Wilson said. “As mayor, I am very committed to taking comprehensive action, not just to balance the budget for the next biennium, but to ensure the longer-term fiscal health of our city.”

Wilson served on the Seattle Revenue Stabilization Workgroup in 2023, a group that looked into new revenue options for the City, and she ran on a platform of being willing to raise new progressive revenue to continue providing City services. However, most of the options on the table for new progressive revenue, including a city-wide capital gains tax, cannot be implemented immediately, with the majority requiring action by the state legislature before they can be adopted.

“[The Mayor] will be transmitting a budget that is making big strides towards sustainability but doesn't solve all of the problems,” Pennucci said. “And one of the things that's been really clear to me in coming back to the City and and working on the budget from the executive branch is that we really need better tools and resources to support a more dynamic budget process that's really focused on how are we getting the best value out of every public dollar, and it needs to be more outcome focused.”

Pennucci shared that in developing the 2027-2028 biennial budget, the office tried to better align budgets to actual spending, looking at budget areas where there has been regular underspend and long term vacancies in order to stretch the City’s dollars further.

The executive order also suggests implementing outcomes-based budget evaluations, which will be led by the Innovation and Performance team in the City budget office. This approach could involve examining all city programs in a specific space to see which ones are having better outcomes, whether there is any overlap between programs, and whether it makes sense to put more money into fewer programs or spread the resources out among many.

Pennucci said her office wants to think carefully about how to measure performance and not use only quantitative methods. In order to do justice to the work, the office plans to only pick one or two program areas to start. Wilson added that it’s important to avoid being simplistic in measuring outcomes.
Wilson did agree that she would be willing to cut programs that aren’t effective.

“We're not talking about trying to whittle down the size of government,” Wilson said. “We're talking about, if we're evaluating programs and we're like: this is the way to solve this problem, then maybe it makes sense to shift some resources from other programs that aren't performing as well into expanding that, and that's just a value question.”

Wilson has spoken before about wanting to show that progressive governance can work, a value she shares with New York Mayor and fellow socialist Zohran Mamdani. Both mayors have evoked allusions to sewer socialism, a movement that focuses on improving public services.

In the first eight months of her term, Wilson has focused on several priorities aimed at improving public services and addressing affordability, including passing a large library levy , putting a transit measure onto the November ballot that would boost frequency on several bus routes, banning junk fees for renters, providing universal school meals , and developing legislation that would ban surveillance pricing on groceries .

Meanwhile, Seattle received the top ranking from The Athletic for its hosting of the World Cup this summer, had no homicides in the month of July , and had its busiest month of visitor foot traffic downtown – in August – since 2019. And Denny Way now has a new bus lane to speed up Route 8, a move applauded by urbanists.

At the same time, Wilson has had her challenges. She’s been criticized for pausing the installation of more surveillance cameras and failing to build a productive relationship with the City Council. She walked back her proposal for a two-year break on builder fees , and she’s had to scale back her goal of opening 4,000 new shelter beds during her first term. Her administration was lambasted by the media for several weeks after a delay in communicating to the public in the aftermath of the Bite of Seattle shooting, even though it appears that SPD held the greater responsibility for the confusion . And her decision to ask SPD’s former Chief Shon Barnes to resign was not universally popular.
This executive order places the focus back on the nuts and bolts of City government, which appear to have been neglected in recent years.
“Some of the very basic things that any organization, whether it's a government, a nonprofit, a business, needs to do well, we don't do well anymore,” Dively said.

Dively said that in addition to saving or reprioritizing dollars, this executive order will set into motion work to ensure the City is complying with all relevant rules and optimizing the resources it has.

Wilson said she wants to use every City dollar as effectively as possible, leaning into efficiency and fiscal responsibility. She knows those terms are generally right-coded but wants to show how they can be brought to bear by a progressive administration to yield positive results.

“For a long time [those terms have] often been used to mean something else,” Wilson said. “Starving government so that it doesn't actually function well, cutting safety net programs, and we're seeing maybe an extreme version of this with the Trump administration, kind of the reductio ad absurdum of this ideology, where you have [...] extreme fiscal irresponsibility paired with slashing services in the most cruel manner and really dismantling important parts of the government apparatus. So I believe that progressive cities like Seattle have both an opportunity and really a responsibility to lead in the other direction.”

The introduction of Wilson’s proposed 2027-2028 budget on Tuesday will kick off two months of discussion as city councilmembers debate what changes they wish to make to the proposal. Given elevated tensions between the Mayor’s Office and City Council, it might prove to be a contentious budget season.
The City Council will need to pass a balanced budget before the end of the year, although they generally make their final budget vote before Thanksgiving.
“This behind-the-scenes work is not flashy,” Wilson said. “But I am committed to leaving city government in better shape than I found it."

articles.title: Housing Advocates, Workers Pack City Hall to Support Temporary Fee Break
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle councilmembers attending a rare late Friday afternoon meeting of the housing committee were met with an overflow crowd last week, and heard over an hour of testimony almost entirely in favor of a temporary discount on housing fees levied on builders. The "Housing Accelerator" proposal, put forward by committee chair Dionne Foster after months of behind-the-scenes negotiations, is intended to rescue a city development pipeline that has all but dried up.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Alongside builders and architects who spent their one minute of testimony laying out the bleak picture of Seattle's current development market were dozens of members of the city's construction trades. Donning hard hats and bright yellow vests, many held up signs that read "Proud YIMBY!" – directly referencing the Yes In By Backyard movement that champions the idea of reducing barriers to market-rate development.

Over the past two years, Seattle has seen a 26% decline in multifamily permitting, in contrast with a 31% increase seen statewide. Those diverging trends have dropped Seattle's share of statewide multifamily permits from 28% in 2024 to 16% now. Those red-alert statistics were presented to the committee by Michael Wilkerson, Director of Economic Research at ECOnorthwest, spelling out the need for a course correction from policymakers.

Under Foster's draft bill, a small constellation of building projects that have already had their permits vested would have access to a 80% discount in fees charged under the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) program – provided they can demonstrate "substantial progress" on construction within two years. The ordinance defines this milestone as passing the first foundation inspection.

New projects entering the pipeline can receive a 60% discount, and will have three years to get to substantial progress, but only if they address the city's relative shortage of family-sized apartments by including at least 25% of units with at least two bedrooms.

New projects do not have the same access to MHA discounts in neighborhoods deemed high risk of displacement, which include Chinatown International District, the Central District, Beacon Hill and urban centers up and down the Rainier Valley. A "legacy homeowner" exception would still grant the discount in those areas if the project site remains in community hands, rather than selling off to an outside developer.

"When a client walks into my office with a desire to build housing on a piece of property and the will to go forward, these days I start that conversation with the absolute certainty that I can get them a permit, I can design their building and they can build it, and if they do that, they will lose money," David Neiman, a partner with Neiman Taber Architects, said during Friday's testimony. "That is an unprecedented situation that I have never seen before in my career."

The hope is that by lowering one major cost component that the city has direct control over will allow more projects will be able to pencil – and bring more frontline construction workers back to jobsites. Developers backing the proposal say they have identified more than 30 stalled projects with vested permits that are ready to deliver more than 6,000 homes should the fee break be enacted, clearing their path to financing.

"We have well over a thousand folks out of work. We haven't seen those numbers since the last recession. So just anything that we can do to spur development, get folks back to work," Billy Hetherington, Political Director for Laborers' Local Union (LiUNA) 242, told The Urbanist . "MHA, the way it's designed, if there's nothing being built, it's not bringing in any money. So, taking a thoughtful reset and looking what happens during that reset, and trying to look at the policy again here in a year or two years to fit it to the right economic climate we're in."
Comments Friday were not universally in support, with some concerns raised about reducing a dedicated revenue source for affordable housing.

"Reducing the City's only housing affordability program is the wrong lever to remove," Alexandra Johnson of the Duwamish River Community Coalition told councilmembers. "MHA, by the City's own study, was 3-5% of total developer costs, and permitting, design reviews, including delays from the city were 9-11%. Rather than committing to reforming internal systems and prioritizing progressive recalibrations of MHA – very similar to what the mayor's taskforce on housing will commit to solving – the city is choosing the least equitable route and a verified ineffective route by the City's own analysis."
So far the proposal appears to have broad support on the council, with Council President Joy Hollingsworth signing on as a co-sponsor.

"The one thing that really stands out the most to me has been the numbers and the data and the hard facts," Hollingsworth said. "My four goals during this process: build more housing, all of it; keep affordable housing in our city as well, to protect those sustainable pathways and funding and operations, long term; protect neighborhoods with high level of risk or displacement; and then also incentivize family-size housing and units. And that's a very thin line to try to navigate. So I really appreciate this conversation."

Paired with the ordinance, which could get a vote as soon as early January, is a companion resolution that has rankled some of the biggest proponents of a potential MHA reduction. It would state the council's intent to study whether the MHA program should be expanded to the city's Neighborhood Residential zones – the formerly single family neighborhoods where a state-mandated upzone unlocked additional density last year.

"I'm trying to set the stage for what our long-term approach looks like. And if you look at the language in the resolution, what you'll see is some significant guardrails in there, including specific language that says we want to direct central staff to develop this in such a way that it does not have a substantial negative impact on development in this area," Foster told The Urbanist following Friday's meeting. "My intent is not to kill housing projects. My intent is housing production and the long-term stability of this funding source in a way that makes sense for the future of our city."

With no MHA fees in place in NR zones but significantly more development capacity, builders often have an incentive to advance a project there rather than in a low-rise (LR) zone closer to transit and amenities, where MHA fees would apply. That disparity, land use committee chair Eddie Lin told The Urbanist, is one reason that he's expressing support for the proposed resolution.

"I think it's worth exploring. I don't see the resolution as a final decision," Lin said. "I think there's some interesting nuances that we could get into there in terms of encouraging greater density. Like, do we encourage lower fees for greater density? Do we look at things like homeowners who might be building for themselves? And so there's a lot to unpack. I just see this as the start of the conversation in trying to build the information that we would need to have a more thoughtful discussion."

With committee work on hold until after Thanksgiving for a full-time focus on the city budget, the Housing Accelerator (with its trailer resolution) is set to come back for additional discussions in December. By that time, the housing committee will have a new member, with District 5 Councilmember Debora Juarez stepping down as soon as special election results in that district are certified.

articles.title: How Do You Heal Contaminated Soil? People Who Work in South End Community Gardens Have Ideas
paras: The South End is one of the most diverse areas in the region. It's also where newborns have a life expectancy that is 11 years shorter than newborns in North Seattle neighborhoods, like Ravenna and Bryant. Factors like access to healthcare and standards of living affect long-term health outcomes, as does pollution from air traffic, cars, and South End industries' byproducts .

This can lead to higher rates of soil contaminants in some areas of the South End compared with other parts of King County, according to a recent analysis by Vedika Bhat, who mapped the results of the King Conservation District's arsenic and lead soil tests. Community gardens can choose to have their soil tested for these two contaminants for free along with having their soils tested for nutrients. Bhat did the community research as part of a University of Washington Environmental and Occupational Health Sciences graduate thesis with Sustainable Seattle.

Outcomes were shared with the community on Sept. 13, when Bhat described the analysis as a comparison of contamination levels between gardens and their neighborhoods. Bhat's analysis showed that arsenic contamination was elevated in several neighborhoods, including the Central District, Mount Baker, and Des Moines. but the levels didn't necessitate cleanup. She said the outcomes of soil samples generally matched patterns of health disparities in the region.

Bhat's maps showed areas in the South End where lead contamination in community garden soils was elevated: the Central District, Mount Baker, Burien, South Park, and Des Moines. Some of the city's neighborhoods have lead levels that should require cleanup according to the Department of Ecology (Madison Park and Montlake and the Fremont/Phinney Ridge/Greenwood area), but there is no agency that mandates who should clean a specific area. (Lead and arsenic also occur naturally in the environment.)

"The difficulty is when our soil is contaminated at cleanup levels, our government supports to resolve this are lacking," said Bhat. "This is where more conversation and push are needed. The solution for gardens is generally raised beds and that takes resources."

Meilani Lanier-Kamaha'o, executive director of Sustainable Seattle, noted, "There are some high-profile sites, like the Duwamish Waterway, which gets a lot of attention, as it ought [to], but then there's less funding-priority energy and resources going to remediate and educate, to protect people most negatively impacted by climate change and environmental issues."

Dr. Melanie Malone, a professor at the University of Washington Bothell School of Interdisciplinary Arts & Sciences, has studied soil contaminants, like lead, arsenic, petroleum products, glyphosate, and many other metals, in the Puget Sound region since 2019. Over the years, her work has expanded. "I started by addressing questions like: What's in my compost? What's in my plants? And then: Is my garden produce safer than what I'm buying at the grocery store?"

Malone says the dangers of contaminants to a body can depend on a number of factors, like what the contaminant is, how often you're exposed to it, what dose you're exposed to, and what point in your life cycle you were in when exposed. Malone noted that babies, older people, and adolescents are more susceptible.

Malone prefers a more progressive and liberatory framing around discussions about exposure. "I don't think it's fair to hide things, especially when people are trying to find a way to protect themselves," said Malone. She recommends communities refer to Dirt Alert to learn more about some recorded contaminants on sites around Tacoma and South King County. She also recommends gardeners use organic compost from sources like FoxFarm and GreenBlenz.
Numerous organizations are trying to address elevated levels of soil contaminants in their gardens.

One South End land-healing project sits near the Duwamish River in South Park. The Duwamish Tribe is rematriating 3.5 acres of land at The Heron's Nest , where the land purchased by Shared Spaces Foundation is being returned to the stewardship of the Duwamish people. The site, located near the Duwamish Longhouse and Cultural Center , was an illegal dumping ground for years. Since 2020, The Heron's Nest has been cleaning the space. Joselynn Tokashiki, The Heron's Nest manager and liaison to the Duwamish Tribe, noted that The Heron's Nest has undergone many soil tests because cars had been abandoned on the land and a neighboring concrete industry had deposited highly toxic kiln dust in the adjacent greenbelt. Kiln dust is a known source of contaminants, like silica, chromium, and cadmium.

Even with that history, the site received a clean bill of health from the Department of Ecology, but The Heron's Nest has continued to test the site and any soil and compost brought onto the land. Tokashiki calls beds with more toxins "spicy." They said they have baseline data on four spicy beds. Two have sunflowers growing in them for phytoremediation, and they'll try growing oyster mushrooms in the other two with added lime to raise the pH, activating the plants to absorb more lead.

Tokashiki said, "[At The Heron's Nest,] there's a lot of healing that the land has done [through our communities], and there's a lot of healing that the land offers to our community. There's beautiful reciprocation that happens through this relationship."
"The soil at Wa Na Wari resulted on the lower end of the high range for lead [contamination]," said Daelen Gates, facilitator for BLOOM , a program centered on gardening as a form of social justice.

C. Davida Ingram founded BLOOM during the pandemic, a time of rising youth suicide rates. Ingram was working at The Seattle Public Library and started the program so youth could be in community while they learned leadership skills and grew vegetables in Wa Na Wari's backyard. When testing revealed contaminated soil, BLOOM increased the number of raised beds.
"There was a disproportionate amount of cancer in my family because of crop dusting in Arkansas fields where my family grew their food," said Ingram.
"When I moved to Seattle, I found this region dealing with concurrent crises in how we've treated our Indigenous populations, Black and Brown communities, and that's built into our soil."

In an area where the soil was highly contaminated, Christina Chambers helped create a healing garden with Indigenous mentors, like Ixtli White Hawk and Pah-tu Pitt . They grew collard greens, wildflowers, and sunflowers to absorb toxins as a form of bioremediation . People who work in the space also wear long sleeves, long pants, gloves, and close-toed shoes.

Chambers' family comes from Africatown near Mobile, Alabama, a place settled by people who were transported on the Clotilda, the last slave ship to the U.S. The community there also struggles with air, water, and ground pollutants from neighboring industries .
In the garden at Wa Na Wari, BLOOM facilitator Gates pointed at the healing garden. "We're growing pumpkins over there to carve, and lavender smells beautiful in the house."

Lynda Wong, a Beacon Hill resident and program manager for SeaTac Airports Community Coalition for Justice (STACK for J) , got involved in South End environmental issues because she and her father faced overhead airplane noise as they worked in their garden. Wong had to speak loudly to compete with the noise, and she began to lose her voice. She started to inform neighbors about air traffic pollution. "While talking with some seniors, some Laotian elders asked if their soil is safe to grow food," said Wong. Now, she works with a number of gardens in southeast Seattle to inform groups about soil contamination in addition to Sea-Tac International Airport's expansion plans .

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, September 21–September 27
articles.author: Dylan Bueche, Shannon Lubetich, Amanda Manitach, and Megan Seling
paras: (MUSIC) Listening to Arlo Parks has always felt like dappled sunlight falling on leaves to me. The English musician is known for emotionally stirring songs with narrative lyrics, often pausing her concerts to read a handwritten poem from a well-worn notebook. Parks makes a mix of indie pop and R&B, but her latest record integrates electronic elements, drawing influence from the nightlife scene in LA, which she moved to in 2022. The tracks on Ambiguous Desire hypnotize the listener as they transition seamlessly between twinkling piano, sparkling synths, and ethereal vocals. The album was co-produced by Parks’s long-time friend and collaborator Baird, who opens the show with a solo set of spacey R&B-influenced pop-rock tunes. ( Showbox SoDo, 8 pm, all age s) SHANNON LUBETICH

(MUSIC) Florida, the syphilitic penis rotting the brain of our country, has given us a plethora of cathartic, captivating punk rock through the years. Against Me!, Hot Water Music, Less Than Jake (lol jk), and Gouge Away, a band that simultaneously sounds like it sprouted from the Washington, DC post-punk scene circa 2001 while also recalling the more guitar-driven wall of noise aspects of the coincidentally vaginal bands Mannequin Pussy and Perfect Pussy, with GA vocalist Christina Michelle’s lung-purging hollers hitting just as hard as Meredith Graves’ famous distorted rage. Also on the bill are Seattle’s Cherub Chains, a hardcore band Asian Verified columnist Michael Wong turned me onto when he described seeing them live for the first time thusly: “The sound was raw, thunderous, a wall of riffs that collapsed into screaming urgency. [Vocalist Molly Nguyen] let out the kind of rallying cry that is hard to make out among the chaos, but the emotions are indelible. You feel it in your chest before your brain catches up.” ( Substation, 7 pm, 18+ ) MEGAN SELING

(VISUAL ART) I regret all the William Kentridge prints I never bought at Kucera Gallery—which have been all of them, unfortunately. Kentridge is a renowned South African contemporary artist whose utterly prolific work ranges from opera productions and animated films (made by repeatedly erasing and redrawing the same palimpsest page) to sculpture and drawing. The work is often rooted in sociopolitical critique of apartheid and industrial exploitation, but also delves into the intimate ineffables of time and memory. His works on paper are deliciously wry, erudite, and kind of punk rock all at once, often involving layers of text and subtext—like linocuts and lithographs printed on actual pages of the Oxford English Dictionary . Learn from my mistake and take one home. Extra credit: The gallery will be screening Kentridge’s feature documentary, Anything Is Possible , on September 23 at 6 pm. ( Greg Kucera Gallery, 6 pm ) AMANDA MANITACH

(PERFORMANCE) The longest-running sketch comedy festival in the US and a certifiably good way to spend an evening underneath Pike Market, Sketchfest 2026 has everything from deranged live sketches to musical numbers and celebrity impressions from local and touring groups. Unlike improv, sketch comedy somewhat mercifully involves skits that have been rehearsed, and someone has actually checked that they are funny and cohesive before performing them live in front of strangers. It’s hosted at the Unexpected Productions Market Theater in Post Alley, and features 20-plus different acts across four nights including solo performances by touring comedians like Cam Wyllie and sketches by writers/producers of The Daily Show and The Tonight Show ! ( Unexpected Productions, 7 pm ) DYLAN BUECHE

(FILM) The world was very different when Dan Savage introduced an amateur porn film festival to curious Seattleites in 2005. That same year, George W. Bush began his second term as the President of the United States, North Korea announced they had nuclear weapons, and Hurricane Katrina devastated the US Gulf Coast. That was also the year the first video was uploaded to YouTube. Online streaming services were distant glimmers of possibility. In fact, all HUMP! submissions that year—Savage remembers receiving about 50 total—were sent to the Stranger offices via mail on VHS tapes, and all evidence was destroyed after the final screening. Now, HUMP! is held twice a year and shown in more than 40 cities around the globe. Participants have upped their production and imagination, and, once COVID-19 hit, they also signed release forms allowing their work to be shown in a streaming library so fans can HUMP! at home. (And yup, they get a cut of the profits.) The 2026 fall lineup, running into October at On the Boards, is all new from anything ever shown before, with films featuring everything from a dim sum table to LEGOs and… Frankenstein’s monster? ( On the Boards, 6:30 pm & 9 pm, 21+ ) MEGAN SELING

(SCIENCE/ART) My memory is hazy, but I’m pretty sure I screamed the first time I saw one of Tyler Thrasher’s crystallized cicadas. It was gorgeous. The bug’s body was completely engulfed with hunks of vibrant purple crystal, and its lacy wings shimmered with delicate shards of stone. It looked like something you’d see flying around planet Thra. Over the years, Thrasher has crystallized scorpions, snail shells, butterflies, stick bugs, snake skeletons, and mummified baby chameleons, and in recent years he’s gotten into “moonbeam flora,” dried plants and flowers coated with various mineral powders that make them glow otherworldly colors in the dark. Daylight saving time ends soon. Prepare for the dark season by filling your space with shimmery, bright, weird things. ( Ghost Gallery, 4–8 pm, all ages, free ) MEGAN SELING

(MUSIC) Kehlani’s been making smooth and soulful R&B since they competed on America’s Got Talent as part of a teen pop group 15 years ago. And though they’ve been nominated for a smattering of awards since, they haven’t taken home many—until this year. Following the release of their self-titled fifth album, they won Best Female R&B/Pop Artist at the BET Awards and the record’s single “Folded” earned Grammys for Best R&B Performance and Best R&B Song. Judging by the music video for that track and their BET Awards performance , I expect a mesmerizing concert experience filled with costume changes, backup dancers, and dramatic ambience. Kehlani’s powerful and vulnerable vocals get me every time, whether they’re singing a downtempo breakup track or a joyful celebration of love. ( Climate Pledge Arena, 6:30 pm, all ages ) SHANNON LUBETICH

articles.title: Slog AM: Snot-nosed, Unvaccinated Kindergarteners, Fewer Teachers for Them to Sicken, Big Crane Goes to Japan
articles.author: Vivian McCall
paras: Most students in Washington State are vaccinated, but rates are falling among kindergarteners , reflective of a nationwide trend. This year, 90.3 percent of the state’s K-12 students met all vaccination requirements. Kindergarteners lagged 3.8 percent behind at 86.5 percent. Whereas overall vaccination rates increased by 0.6 percent over last year, vaccination rates for Kindergarteners fell by 0.6 percent. It makes some sense that we’d see the effects of years of anti-vax bullshit in families with the youngest children. State vaccine teams are keeping a particularly close eye on measles-mumps-rubella shots. Once eliminated domestically, measles clusters are erupting all over the country. This American Life had a great story about how the town of Vernal, Utah ended its outbreak in six weeks.

Driven by budget pressures —and the Legislature consistently underfunding education—schools across Washington State are starting the fall semester with fewer staff and teachers. We’re facing a budget shortfall , so this problem will likely worsen.

Unions are spending big to save the Millionaires Tax from the likes of Brian Heywood & Co. for the simple reason that this state fucking needs money for the public sector and graduated income taxes are unconstitutional. For now . We over rely on sales tax and fund every little thing with a property tax levy. “We think it’s entirely reasonable to ask the wealthiest among us to pay a little bit more,” said Adam Glickman, SEIU 775 secretary-treasurer, who told the Seattle Times union caregivers pay 16 percent of their $22 an hour income on taxes, while the state’s richest people pay only three percent.

As President Donald Trump runs t oward the sensual, robotic arms of AI companies, his base is backing away, WIRED reports. More than 60 percent of Americans, and 47 percent of Republicans, oppose data center construction; in August, “the National Republican Senatorial Committee sent a private memo to AI companies sounding the alarm on how voters perceive data centers, warning that ‘campaign or party committees can not fix the toxic brand of an entire segment of the economy.’” Last week, GOP strategist Tony Fabrizio told party candidates in a memo that “unqualified support” for data centers is a “losing position.”

President Trump, man of the people, voice of the voiceless, overclass hero, wrote on Truth Social in August that “only the backwards and poor” would oppose data centers in their town, and he hasn’t shut up about it since. The thousands of negative comments left on a pro-AI post he made on his own platform last week outnumbered positive comments four to one , a New York Times analysis found . In Trump’s increasingly vacant eyes, backing off AI only means losing to China.

CNN, MS Now, and Politico are suing over the White House access they were stripped of on Saturday because of “fake news.” The networks are expected to file the lawsuit later this morning, and the White House had no comment. Trump did, on Truth Social: “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” the president said in his totally believable post post. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

What a surprise, Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party is dominating the vote in the first tightly controlled parliamentary election since starting a war in Ukraine (most antiwar candidates have been barred from the ballot). The Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the ultra-nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, New People, A Just Russia, whose members vote with United Russia most of the time, are also expected to pick up seats.

More than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by fighting on the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognized government of Yemen that does not control the capital, Sana’a, or the vast majority of the country’s population, is using drones and missiles to strike the flat coastal plains where the Houthi “rebels” are digging in, the BBC reports .

What comes up must come down: The orange-and-white crane that towered 500 feet above the Big Pasco Industrial Center in the Tri-Cities for the last 15 years is being dismantled and sent to Japan to construct nuclear power plants. The crane’s Japanese owner ordered the crane from maker Lampson International 20 years ago, but the crane stayed in Pasco because Japan paused its nuclear program after the 2011 earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear plant disaster in Fukushima. Now that the country’s nuclear age has resumed, the crane will spend seven years building the Higashidori Nuclear Power Station for Tokyo Electric in the northern Aomori Prefecture.
Weather: Mostly cloudy, then sunny. Tomorrow, on the first day of fall, there’s a 20 percent chance of rain. I feel the chill returning.

paras: The longest-running hotel workers’ strike in Washington’s history came to a close when Hilton and its workers agreed to a contract earlier this month. We previously reported on the workers’ efforts and concerns ahead of the World Cup. Now, we’re bringing you an update with what’s in the workers’ new contract.
The first strike Aspen Desmarais joined turned out to be historic.

“85 days was a lot. It was in the first couple of weeks. It was really fun. And then for a second there, it felt really hard fought and like what we were doing wasn't getting any impact. But I will not be out stubborn by anyone until I get the things that we need to protect people,” said Desmarais, a bartender at Embassy Suites by Hilton.

Desmarais and other workers went on strike on June 18th during the FIFA Men’s World Cup. The strike lasted a total of 85 days. The union hopes the contract agreement will pave the way for other hotel workers in the state.
Some of the changes in the new agreement include:

Hilton responded to a request for comment, saying: “This agreement reflects a collaborative outcome and our commitment to our valued Team Members. We look forward to welcoming our Team Members back to work and continuing to deliver exceptional hospitality to our guests.”
But for Desmarais, perhaps the biggest win was laying the groundwork to help protect immigrant workers.

“When people come to online commenting about our immigrant workers and being saying that they shouldn't be afraid if they're legal, they are all legal. It's just a scary world and Ice does not care if you're legal or not... In an extremely oppressive system right now towards immigrants. I think any win is a win,” Desmarais said.

Los Tacos No 1 is a classic New York success story. articles.title: Justin Herbert has been the quarterback of tomorrow his entire NFL career. Whose fault is that?
articles.author: Alex Kirshner
paras: The Chargers star is huge, can run and has a golden right arm. But he has never quite reached the heights many expected for him

Justin Herbert is one of the most promising quarterbacks in the NFL. In fact, Justin Herbert has forever been one of the most promising quarterbacks in the NFL. That adjective, “promising”, continued to be load-bearing on Sunday, as Herbert and his Chargers turned in an underwhelming performance in a 26-14 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders. Los Angeles are now 0-2 on the year, with those losses coming to the team who picked No 1 in this year’s draft and a moribund Arizona who picked No 3. Stockholders in Herbert’s growth were taking a beating in after-hours trading. But, as ever, there’s plenty of reason to debate whether Herbert underachieved or whether his team let him down.

Herbert is 6ft 6in, can run, has a golden right arm and is capable of making astonishing throws . NFL decision-makers view him as roughly the sixth-best QB in the league but also say things like , “He should have more accolades at this point.” Certainly, he should have more wins this season, but on Sunday the 28-year-old found himself outdueled by one of the league’s senior citizens in Vegas quarterback Kirk Cousins, 10 years his senior. Herbert completed 15 of 27 passes for a touchdown and two interceptions, and he also took three sacks. Cousins threw a pick and took two sacks but was much more efficient from down to down (8.7 yards per attempt to Herbert’s 7.1). articles.title: When presidents ban journalists from the White House, the First Amendment is not the only constitutional right at stake
articles.author:
<name>Wayne Unger, Associate Professor of Law, Quinnipiac University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/wayne-unger-1503965"/>
paras: The president is going after the press again.

On Sept. 19, 2026, journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico were denied access to the White House after President Donald Trump revoked their credentials , citing “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” On social media, Trump posted, “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President .”

This is not Trump’s first attempt at banning journalists from the White House. During his first term , he sought to ban CNN’s Jim Acosta by revoking his credentials following a contentious news conference about the 2018 midterm elections.

In that conflict, CNN quickly filed a lawsuit, arguing that, “If left unchallenged, the actions of the White House would create a dangerous chilling effect for any journalist who covers our elected officials .”

Journalism organizations also responded. The Committee to Protect Journalists, the Radio Television Digital News Association and even Acosta’s peers at The Daily Caller – a right-leaning news outlet – condemned the White House ban .
A federal court granted CNN a temporary injunction – reinstating Acosta’s press pass. The Trump administration later restored Acosta’s credentials , and CNN dropped its lawsuit.
Many commentators and members of the press have called Trump’s latest ban on the three news organizations a violation of the First Amendment .
White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich said on X, “Today’s action revoking access for journalists from CNN, POLITICO, and MSNOW violates the First Amendment .”

Even George Washington University law professor Jonathan Turley, who staunchly supports Republicans and frequently criticizes the press, said on X that the ban “ would be an assault on long-honored principles of a free press .”

As Turley and many others have argued over the weekend, Trump’s ban is almost certainly unconstitutional under the First Amendment , which states that “Congress shall make no law … abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press.” Media law professor Frank LoMonte argued in 2018, “The First Amendment guarantees all Americans freedom to speak and publish without government interference .”

But they may be missing a crucial point. In fact, there’s more than one constitutional right involved in such a case. The judge who restored Acosta’s press pass in 2018 primarily based his ruling on the reporter’s Fifth Amendment rights to due process, not on the First Amendment.

And in my view as a constitutional law professor, it is less clear whether the press has a constitutional right of access to the White House even though past presidents have honored and respected the press’s access to the executive branch.

While several Supreme Court cases, such as Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia , unequivocally provide the press with a right of access to criminal trials, there is no Supreme Court precedent that specifically provides a clear constitutional right of access to the White House.

In one case from 1977, Sherrill v. Knight , Robert Sherrill, the Washington correspondent for The Nation, was – after holding press passes over several years – denied a press pass because the Secret Service advised he should not be given one. The Secret Service refused to disclose their justification.

Sherrill sued, and the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that the Secret Service cannot deny a White House press pass absent “narrow and specific standards by which applications are to be judged.”

The court required the White House to provide the press with “notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for (them) to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial (of a press pass).”

In the court’s view, these requirements – notice and an opportunity to rebut the bases for the denial of a press pass – are protected by two constitutional guarantees working together, the press protections in the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment’s protections from arbitrary deprivations of “life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.”

In other words, before the federal government can deprive an individual of their life, liberty or property, the federal government must provide that individual with due process , whose purpose is widely accepted as preventing “ arbitrary governmental actions .”
There are a number of Supreme Court decisions that could be key in the current journalists’ lawsuit , which was filed on Sept. 21, 2026.

Among them is Mathews v. Eldridge from 1976, in which the Supreme Court stated that due process is flexible depending on the extent of the liberty or property interest at stake. But in general, the justices said, due process requires the government to provide notice to the individual and an opportunity for the individual to present their case before the deprivation occurs.

In Sherrill v. Knight from 1977, the court ruled that the denial of a press pass implicated a First Amendment liberty interest. That interest, the court wrote, “undoubtedly qualifies as liberty which may not be denied without due process of law under the fifth amendment.”

This nuance – the First and Fifth Amendment working in tandem – is what most commentators and critics are missing in their response to the recent ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico. In fact, these outlets collectively lead with their claim that the Trump administration violated their Fifth Amendment right to due process in their lawsuit to block Trump’s ban .
“Even if attending a White House event is not a constitutionally guaranteed right, that doesn’t mean the government is free to take it away as punishment ,” LoMonte argued in 2018.

Based on public reporting, it is clear that the Trump administration did not provide CNN, MS NOW or Politico with clear written notice stating the reasons for the revocation of their press passes. It certainly did not provide the outlets with an opportunity to rebut Trump’s unsupported claim that they report “FICTION and LIES.”

The same Trump-appointed judge who decided the CNN Acosta case has been assigned to the latest press ban case . So, if the CNN Acosta case is any indication, I expect the federal judge to promptly, but temporarily, reinstate the news outlets’ press passes while Trump tries to argue that his actions are constitutional, which in my view, they are not.
