articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Quiet Zone in Kent
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On August 24, 2026, Kent’s long-awaited Quiet Zone took effect along the BNSF Railway mainline through downtown. This designation, granted by the Federal Railroad Administration in June , no longer requires trains to sound their horn when approaching an at-grade crossing. Over the past 14 years, the City of Kent has worked to meet the necessary requirements to achieve a Quiet Zone. Recent infrastructure upgrades include building raised concrete medians, adding additional signs, and refreshing pavement markings. In a non-Quiet Zone area, all trains are required to sound their horn 15-20 seconds before each street crossing.

The BNSF mainline tracks are used by 38 passenger trains and many more freight trains every day. The frequent at-grade crossings in downtown Kent resulted in nearby residents hearing hundreds of train horns day and night. The Quiet Zone stretches between S 212th St and S 259th St. The following crossings are included:

As safety is still a top priority, train engineers are still allowed to sound the horn in emergency situations or as they deem necessary. While the Quiet Zone is officially in effect, it may take some time for nearby residents to hear a difference. One week after the change was implemented, the Kent Reporter noted that many trains were still using their horn at each crossing. I was in Kent earlier this week and each of the five trains (four Sounder, one Amtrak Cascades) I saw used their horn at each crossing.

articles.title: Traffic Safety Package Advances with Change Targeting Historic Districts
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A three-bill package intended to improve Seattle's response to increasing rates of deaths and serious injuries on city streets was approved by City Council's transportation committee on Thursday. Introduced by committee chair Rob Saka and dubbed the SAFER Streets Act , the proposal largely empowers officials at the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) with explicit authority that they already have the ability to wield. But it also sets up future legislation around post-crash responses and safety upgrades to vehicles used by city contractors.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
The committee approved a raft of amendments before a final vote, tweaks needed in part due to the package's rushed process to get advanced before the council's fall budget work.

Most of these were technical changes that didn't have big policy impacts, but one major amendment, put forward by Alexis Mercedes Rinck and approved on a 3-2 vote, proved contentious. It added a provision explicitly beefing up SDOT's authority to make changes to roadways within the city's historic districts, letting them sidestep an oftentimes lengthy historic board or commission approval process on certain safety-related changes.

Traffic safety advocates had been pushing for the city to receive that authority, in the wake of several high-profile incidents where city projects have met resistance at preservation boards in recent years. This spring, SDOT had to walk back a plan to deploy bike and scooter corrals across Pioneer Square to both keep sidewalks clear of micromobility devices but also to keep intersections clear of parked cars, a treatment known as intersection daylighting. Business owners in the district had raised concerns about aesthetics and lost parking, despite the original plan only involving the removal of one or two legal spots.

Under the amendment, "traffic control devices and spot design changes" in historic districts wouldn't be subject to landmark designation, nor would the city need to receive a Certificate of Approval (which can be appealed) to advance adjustments within Seattle's eight historic districts when it comes to that narrow range of adjustments.

"This amendment focuses on the Traffic Engineer's authority specifically over traffic control devices," Amanda Allen, a legislative analyst at the City, told councilmembers. "It does not include bollards, which may be of interest to folks, it is really focused on signs, signals, and markings."

Ahead of the vote, advocates of historic districts across the city showed up to testify at city hall in opposition to the change. Comments regarding Pioneer Square and Pike Place were the most prevalent, but they also included concerns about Ballard Avenue and Chinatown-International District.

"We believe safety and preservation are not in conflict, and they have not been historically," Alliance for Pioneer Square Executive Director Lisa Howard said during public comment, suggesting that this move had been put forward in response to the scooter corral incident alone. "We can make our streets safer without eliminating meaningful review in our historic districts."

Advocates have argued the corral debacle is far from an isolated incident. In 2024, SDOT was forced to negotiate with the Pioneer Square Preservation Board over a two-block protected bike connection along Yesler Way between Occidental Avenue and Western Avenue, the only direct bike lane planned between the waterfront and central downtown. An initial presentation noted construction could have started as soon as July of that year, but the department was forced to come back for a second meeting in the fall, after potential issues were raised about driver access to I-5 from the neighborhood.
In the end, the connection did not go in until early 2026, and with a last-minute adjustment to retain a potentially dangerous left turn in response to "community feedback."

Inside Pike Place Market, this adjustment would likely not give SDOT unilateral authority to keep vehicle traffic out of the Market, in the wake of recent historical commission approval of three-day "soft closures" every week through the winter, ramping down a successful Pike Place pedestrianization pilot. But it would give the department more tools than it has currently.
In putting forward her amendment, Rinck expressed support for the city's historic districts, but spelled out the need to elevate safety issues above other changes within those districts.

"I hope we can agree that some things are just too important to subject to the Seattle Process, and I believe traffic safety meets that bar," Rinck said. "I've been told this amendment goes too far, but I dare to say the city has not gone far enough when it comes to preventing traffic deaths and injuries. So I hope people hear today that my bringing this amendment forward is in response to the calls for decisive action that I've heard from families who have lost loved ones on our streets, our transit advocates, and everyone who has had too close of a call."

While Rinck's amendment did pass, there are outstanding questions about whether it is fully implementable as written. It does not make any changes to the section of city code directly governing historic districts, and it would take a completely different bill with a different subject to make those updates. In addition, District 2 Councilmember Eddie Lin suggested an additional carveout might be necessary for Chinatown-International District, which was included on a list of the 11 most endangered historic places in the U.S. in 2023.
But Lin, along with amendment co-sponsor Dionne Foster, voted to give the amendment the green light for now.

"I do think there's a way to to do historic preservation and achieve public safety, but I do think at the end of the day, the authority needs to lie with with who is responsible, and that is, in my opinion, the traffic engineer," Lin said. "The traffic engineer should, whenever possible, take into consideration any recommendations and feedback so that it's consistent with the historic preservation. At the end of the day, the traffic engineer is responsible for traffic safety, and we have seen in in polling, how traffic safety in recent years has been the number one public safety concern, and there's good reason behind that."

Bob Kettle, who represents the district that includes Pike Place Market, raised issues with the process to review the amendment, as well as a lack of outreach to the specific districts that would be impacted in voting against the amendment.

"As it relates to the legislative process, I am a little bit astonished that we're looking at an amendment that was not seen by our in-house legal counsel until this morning. There was issues in the city attorney's office with its review. There was no consideration of the state pieces, state law, and the like," Kettle said. "And as it relates to stakeholdering, I don't think obviously – Pike Place Market wasn't stakeholdered, Pioneer Square wasn't stakeholdered. I tend to doubt that Chinatown International District was stakeholdered on this."

Saka, who also voted no, said that this potential tweak had come up during the development of the overall package, and had been suggested directly by SDOT as a potential reform. But he did state that he could support a more narrowly tailored amendment that didn't treat all of the eight historic districts the same.

"I declined to accept it for a reason," Saka said. "I do appreciate the the intent [or] spirit here behind this, and we need to have tough policy conversations and be willing to do things up to and including this at some point, I just don't think we've done the the work and stakeholdering to do that. I know my constituents in Pioneer Square don't like this, even though I know they strongly support safety."

It is likely that the proposal sees some modifications ahead of a vote of the full council set for mid-October, including potential changes that involve notification of the historic boards on projects that may no longer require direct approval.

"It's critical that we have clarity around the role of the City Traffic Engineer and their authority to make decisions around safety, so that we can work towards the goals that we all share when it comes to traffic safety, public safety, and Vision Zero," Dionne Foster said. "I intend to bring an amendment to full council that commits SDOT to providing notification to the historic boards of significant changes to traffic control devices within the historic districts. I believe in this way we can ensure that we have clarity on the decision making as well as clarity on the information sharing."

articles.title: Deconstruction Is a Key Frontier for Climate Action in Seattle
articles.author: Syris Valentine
paras: Aaron Blanchard recalls taking a tour through the broken-open guts of a building across from the downtown ferry terminal with a crew from Dixon Demolition as they prepared to take the building down. Crawling through holes in the walls to move from section to section, he was struck by all the immense, exposed timbers that framed and supported the structure.

“Normally, there’s all this drywall,” Blanchard said. “There’s all this other stuff you’ve got to deal with.” But in that building, it was nothing but lumber, and Blanchard wanted to make sure none of it went to the landfill.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

[Note: This article is a follow up to a three-part series on Seattle’s Climate Action Plan. Part One: The history of climate action in Seattle . Part Two: The current state of climate action in Seattle . Part Three: Climate action for a resilient Seattle .]

Salvage assessments like that are required in Seattle before any building comes down or undergoes a substantial alteration. As director of operations and part-owner of Earthwise Architectural Salvage — a company with 35 years in the salvaging business — Blanchard has supported plenty of these assessments, looking for anything worth saving that he can either resell as is or remanufacture for sale. Cabinets, doors, windows, and the like are all that’s worth prying out of most prospective demolitions for Earthwise. Other than that, it’s just loads of drywall and two-by-four lumber.

But when Blanchard walked through this particular building along Alaskan Way, he saw little that wasn’t worth saving. He turned to the demolition contractor and said: “You guys know this is going to be a deconstruction, right? You’re gonna save so much of this wood, and we’re gonna buy it from you.”

To dangle an extra carrot, Blanchard told them about Seattle Public Utilities’ (SPU’s) deconstruction incentive , which provides contractors with $6,000 per commercial project when the building is taken down board by board and beam by beam. That incentive typically only covers a slim, single digit percentage of a project’s cost, but deconstruction offers its own ways for contractors to cut costs and recoup expenses. Crews don’t need to pay the tonnage fee of shipping waste to the landfill, and they can get some additional cash back when they sell salvaged materials to a company like Earthwise.

This incentive is one of several bids on the part of SPU to promote a circular economy in Seattle. Creating pathways that divert materials from the landfill and instead cycle through the economy in different forms has recently gained increased attention inside the City. Late last year, the Office of Sustainability and Environment (OSE) began the process to revamp the citywide climate action plan. That effort means more than simply updating goals and timelines; they’re incorporating new areas of focus into the plan as well. They presented the action areas for public discussion during a July forum . One area looked squarely at how the City can “reuse more, waste less.”

The motivation for this comes from a simple fact that many within the climate sphere used to overlook. “Climate change is a product not only of greenhouse gas emissions, but the amount of economic activity,” Deric Gruen, a co-founder of the nonprofit Peoples Economy Lab, told The Urbanist

If people repair, reuse, repurpose, and even simply share more , then they not only prevent waste from piling up in landfills already nearing capacity , they also reduce the need to open up more minelands, log more forests, or extract more fossil fuels with all the environmental damages they bring.

In Seattle, circularity gained steam after a 2023 exercise in which OSE and SPU partnered together to consider how the picture of Seattle’s emissions changes when we look beyond transportation, buildings, and municipal waste alone to factor in how eating habits, purchasing patterns, travel plans, and household activities shape global warming, even when the associated carbon enters the atmosphere far outside city limits. This approach is called a consumption-based emissions inventory .

SPU wanted to understand how consumption in Seattle affected the city’s climate footprint and “how our work around waste prevention and changing the way that we think about materials can support the broader global emissions reduction efforts,” said SPU’s circular economy policy advisor Ashima Sukhdev.
“It totally shifts the strategy,” Gruen said. “A consumption-based inventory asks, how are we meeting our needs and what’s our responsibility for that whole supply chain?”

This requires City officials to think about what can be done to lessen the imprint left on the environment by every aspect of a resident’s life. Much of the work that goes into the circular economy thinks about all the things that people engage with and dispose of on a daily basis: food, clothes, dishware, and the like. For instance, since 2022, SPU has led the Reuse Seattle partnership that aims to replace single-use containers across Seattle’s cafes, restaurants, and event venues with reusable alternatives .

This summer, SPU and the Office of Economic Development also helped Seattle Reconomy to open the Reuse Commons in Lake City where nonprofits, businesses, and community organizations can host events, provide mutual support, and work under one roof to make it easy as possible for people in the community to engage with the circular economy. In its final form, the commons would operate as a sort of mall.

“Imagine somebody comes into the reuse commons, drops off their kids' goods, their bike, their tools, their furniture. We take that, we organize it and redistribute it,” Josh Epstein, the executive director of Seattle Reconomy, told The Urbanist . “And on the other side of the reuse commons is our storefront where we're selling fixed, upcycled furniture and art and bikes and tools.”
The commons would also provide a new space for Reconomy’s central offering: sharing libraries where members can borrow tools, dishware, basic appliances, and other common goods.

Epstein believes the Reuse Commons represents a huge opportunity for residents of Lake City and North Seattle, and it also could provide a model for something that Seattle Reconomy and partners like the Furniture Repair Bank could recreate in South Seattle .

Projects like these with a focus on consumer goods can help, but advocates like Dave Bennink see the biggest potential for reducing waste and society’s burden on the environment as lying in the built environment, in particular by thinking about construction and demolition in new ways—by thinking about deconstruction.

The average American generates 4.9 pounds of trash per day , adding up to around 141,000 pounds in a lifetime. It’s a staggering number that numerous organizations in the city , state , and country are working to drive down. But as Bennink, the director of the Building Deconstruction Institute, pointed out in a conversation with The Urbanist , the average home in America weighs between 80,000 and 160,000 pounds . So, demolishing a home is a great way to speed-run the waste budget of your life.

“It doesn't matter how many bottles you recycle and how many newspapers you recycle,” said Bennink, “if you choose to demolish your building, then you have wasted an entire lifetime's worth of materials.” To solve the issue, his company has helped prove out a workable alternative: “We don't demolish [buildings]. We disassemble them.”

As a national expert in deconstruction, Bennink has helped train contractors across 45 states, five provinces, and nine countries, and he has advised at least 22 municipalities — including Portland, Seattle, and King County — considering policies and programs to grow local deconstruction industries. The collective impact he and his team have accomplished since Bennink started this work in 1993 has been immense: Across more than 5,000 projects, Bennink’s team has diverted more than 100 million pounds from the landfill and reclaimed wood and lumber equivalent to 10,000 acres of standing forest. But his work advising policies and helping entrepreneurs start their own circular businesses has the potential to multiply that impact.

Of course, it’s all well and good to reclaim wood, but the real impact comes when that wood is reused, both Bennink and Blanchard pointed out. For someone like Bennink who has been in the business for decades and helped foster an ecosystem around him of people bought into reclaiming and reusing lumber, it’s easy enough to find a new building to take whatever is extracted from an old one.
“If we remove some wood flooring from one home,” Bennink said, “then we have someone in our group of businesses now that will reinstall it in somebody else's home.”

But creating that kind of ecosystem requires a lot of capacity that many contractors may not have. “If your model is selling the wood to make up the difference between demolition and deconstruction,” Blanchard said, “well, now you also have to have a lumber company.”

That’s why the City of Seattle, with the support of a $4 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency, partnered with Earthwise to open a new Salvage Lumber Warehouse in SoDo earlier this year . It provides a simple destination for contractors to sell what wood they save, and then it’s up to Earthwise to find a customer for it. Most of those customers are homeowners and business owners working on smaller projects.

With all the benefits that come from deconstruction, some environmentalists have argued it should be a requirement, and some cities have taken the plunge with their own versions of such mandates . In 2016, Portland became the first city in the nation to establish an ordinance requiring deconstruction, specifically on all buildings built before 1940.

Since then, cities like Boulder, Colorado; Palo Alto, California; San Antonio, Texas; and Baltimore, Maryland, have instituted their own versions of such an ordinance. In contrast, Seattle still relies on an incentive, which has been used sparingly thus far. Just 45 projects have used that incentive since it launched, according to SPU. In that same time, SPU has issued 750 demolition permits for single family homes alone.

While having just 6% of homes deconstructed instead of demolished feels low given the potential impact that this can bring, Blanchard pointed out that not every building has materials that are worth saving, which can make an ordinance with mandatory salvage rates tricky to implement. It could easily mean you’re saving heaps of wood that no one wants to buy, so they just end up languishing in a warehouse instead of the landfill.
“You need to balance the new supply that you will be creating of reclaimed materials with a new demand,” Bennink added.

Integrating reclaimed lumber into other projects, whether new construction or renovation, is where the real environmental benefits of this practice shows up. According to one study , when reclaimed wood is used in a project instead of virgin timber, the net demand for energy is 13 times lower and the total emissions are five times lower as well.

Ensuring there is demand for those materials, however, means that a city must ease its way into any sort of mandate. That’s why when Portland was first considering its ordinance, Bennink recommended they start with an incentive. An incentive period gives all parties involved in the built environment time to understand what deconstruction means for properties around the city and what it takes to be successful in that project. More importantly, it helps the industry to levelize costs and timing with traditional demolitions.

Because deconstruction can require more labor power and specialized skills, some firms feel justified in charging extra to dismantle a building in that way — even when they have opportunities to cut other costs and gain additional incomes. But Bennink’s vision is for deconstruction costs to be less than traditional demolition.
“We don't want it to cost more,” he said. “We don't want it to take more time. We don't want to adversely affect people's projects.”

Bennink has spent three decades refining his methods to ensure deconstruction can be done economically, and when he trains local workforces, as he has done in Portland and King County, he tries to impart those skills onto others. When The Urbanist spoke with Bennink, he was in the middle of taking apart a pole barn.
“We were half the price of demolition,” he said. “For other buildings, we might be 25% more than the price of demolition, and on lots of buildings we are equal to the price.”

So with a relatively new deconstruction trade emerging in Seattle, costs might currently be higher than demolition in many cases, but if the City increases use of its incentive or begins to transition to a mandate on some projects, those cost disparities should narrow in the coming years. Boosting the use of deconstruction and salvage across the city’s building stock could end up being an important part of Seattle’s climate strategy, and potentially the City’s upcoming update to its climate action plan.

articles.title: Seattle Is Poised to Ban Supermarket Algorithmic Price Discrimination
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: This coming Tuesday, in an effort to crack down on price gouging and discrimination, the Seattle City Council will vote on a bill prohibiting large grocery store companies from using customer personal information to customize prices and discounts.

Proposed by Mayor Katie Wilson and Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, the legislation will require grocery stores with more than 20 locations worldwide to stop using personal data to set individualized prices and discounts. It would also apply to third party delivery apps such as Instacart, as well as mixed-used stores like Target.

The idea that grocery companies are charging different people different prices based on their past purchases sounds like a futuristic dystopia. But it’s not far off. The practice isn’t in brick and mortar stores yet, but it’s a widespread reality for online shopping. And they’ve already been hoarding your data for years.

Back in 2019, the marketing arm of Kroger, the supermarket giant that owns QFC and Fred Meyer, boasted about collecting more than 2,000 data points on customers using past purchasing history and information bought from data brokers. That data will feed the new pricing algorithms.

Those algorithms are designed to estimate a customer’s purchasing power and how willing they might be to pay more. As part of a Consumer Reports study last year, 39 volunteers loaded up virtual Instacart baskets of products from a Seattle Safeway store. They received a range of prices from $114 to $124 for the exact same goods. That study estimated that this type of price manipulation, if applied to a family of four, could result in cost differences as high as $1,200 a year.

While currently algorithmic pricing is mainly limited to online shopping and loyalty apps, it’s right around the corner for brick-and-mortar stores with the introduction of electronic price labels , which allow stores to instantly change prices of goods. The city council ordinance will require these labels to be the same for different customers.

Uptown QFC cashier and florist Kristen Wilder told The Stranger that Kroger already started rolling out these electronic labels at her store in July. She says customers already hate that they can only access most coupons through an app which collects their data, and she’s worried about the impact of the new labels if the bill doesn’t pass. Wilder’s union, UFCW 3000, has been a key backer of the legislation.

Kerem Levitas, a senior policy advisor in Mayor Wilson’s office says Seattle would be the first city to enact a ban on grocery algorithmic price discrimination, though Portland and New York City are already working on similar legislation. This wouldn’t be entirely novel. Maryland, New Jersey, and Connecticut have already passed similar statewide regulations. The City’s legislation is partially based on a similar statewide bill introduced this year that did not pass.

Washington People’s Privacy founder Maya Morales believes the Seattle bill could be the most comprehensive. It doesn’t allow exemptions for individualized discounts, which can be used to get around fair pricing rules.

“What happens is people are offered these individualized discounts, but often they’ve used a deceptive pricing model and a deceptive discount model to actually end up with customers paying more,” Morales said. So even if the prices are the same, allowing customized coupons would still allow companies to discriminate.

Under the ordinance, large grocery store companies will have to offer discounts based on equal criteria. So, if you get a buy-one-get-one-free deal for accruing a certain amount of loyalty points, other customers must also receive the same deal. Discounts based on certain allowable characteristics—deals for seniors, for veterans—would still be allowed, as long as everyone in that category receives it.

Because company algorithms are proprietary, it’s hard for independent auditors to read the source code and see if they are violating civil rights laws. Morales argues that the only way to prevent pricing discrimination based on race or other protected classes is by banning individualized pricing altogether.

Predictably, big grocers are mad. Grocery store lobby groups are flooding city council with testimony asking for a personalized discounts loophole. The Northwest Grocery Retail Association even employed a mass texting service to ask Seattleites to send letters to the council. The form email is definitely not astroturfed: “Please amend the ordinance to make the rules clear: don’t use my information to charge me more, but don’t prevent it from being used to help me save.”
The Northwest Grocery Retail Association did not respond to a request for comment.

Lead sponsor Rinck says she hasn’t any constituents in favor of having their data used to get personalized discounts. In fact, she said the vast majority of real-life people who are showing up at public comment support the legislation.

“When I talk to people, they’ve expressed to me a lot of discomfort with how their data is now being used and how it could be used against them,” Rinck said. “The price of groceries should be based on the product, not on who the shopper is or what an algorithm thinks they will pay.”
The post Seattle Is Poised to Ban Supermarket Algorithmic Price Discrimination appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: Two Oregon lawmakers want to end an unusual exemption in the state’s records law that has kept the public from learning how hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer money is spent on subsidized housing — and the effort has already landed key industry support.

Rep. Pam Marsh, chair of Oregon’s House Committee on Housing and Homelessness, told ProPublica that she plans to introduce legislation next year to eliminate a law that shields key details of state spending on low-income housing .

The southern Oregon Democrat said she didn’t realize the documents were being kept secret until reading about it in a ProPublica story. She said previous leaders of her committee told her they were also unaware.
“I think this is an issue that will have very broad interest,” Marsh said.
State Sen. Khanh Pham, a Portland Democrat and chair of the Senate Committee on Housing and Development, said she also wants the Legislature to tackle the issue in its next session.

Meanwhile, a lobbying group for low-income housing developers, lenders and related businesses, Housing Oregon, said it strongly supports repealing the secrecy provision; the organization has asked the state to disclose more about projects that it funds in the meantime.

“Oregon’s affordable housing providers share the public’s interest in ensuring that public investments in housing are used effectively, responsibly, and with visibility,” said Kevin Cronin, a spokesperson for the group. “The questions raised in your recent ProPublica article regarding development costs deserve serious attention.”
Cronin said Oregon can increase transparency around development costs “while still protecting genuinely proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”
“More consistent reporting of costs and outcomes will help policymakers, providers, researchers, and the public understand where the system is working and where it needs improvement,” Cronin said.

ProPublica highlighted Oregon’s secrecy around low-income housing in August. Since 2021, our story noted, Oregon has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each low-income apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for another $850 million in future state funding, and costs are expected to continue rising.

“We are spending, as you said, a lot of money on the development of affordable housing,” Marsh said. “We really need to understand what it is that we’re funding, how much it costs, why it costs that much, and be able to justify the investments that we’re making.”
In other states, researchers and journalists have used the financial records from subsidized housing projects to investigate their spiraling costs and the drivers behind the growing price tag.

Marsh said after reading the ProPublica story that she “pretty much immediately” looked up the provision in Oregon public records law that officials cite for keeping cost details secret. She said financial documents that show where a project’s money is coming from and what it’s going to should be public and easily accessed. She said she would like to see them posted online as part of the public materials that Oregon’s Housing Stability Council receives for each project before awarding subsidies.

Pham, in a written statement, said: “It’s imperative that Oregonians can trust that our state government is investing in affordable housing as cost-effectively as possible. I appreciated ProPublica’s reporting on Oregon’s inadequate public records law that hinders our ability to monitor how affordable housing funds are being spent, and I’m hopeful legislators can address this next year.”

Oregon’s Sunshine Committee, which reviews public records exemptions and recommends ones that could be rolled back, is also examining the exemption for housing financials as a result of ProPublica’s coverage, co-chair Charlie Fisher said.

It’s not clear where opposition to repeal efforts, if any, might arise. Officials in Washington and California, where the details of state spending on subsidized housing are available to the public, have said it hasn’t interfered with low-income housing efforts.

Oregon Housing and Community Services, the state housing agency that persuaded lawmakers to create the records exemption in 1997, cited the law in redacting major sections of developers’ cost reports that ProPublica requested in May.
The agency’s current executive director, Andrea Bell, told ProPublica in July that she is committed to transparency but that the agency is following the law as it stands today.

Asked to comment this week about whether the agency would support efforts to change the law, a spokesperson said by email that state agencies don’t take positions on bills. “OHCS appreciates the opportunity to review the legislation” that’s introduced in 2027, the spokesperson wrote.

articles.title: Kitsap Transit adds bus service, reduces ferry service in Fall service change
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Kitsap Transit’s Fall 2026 service change began yesterday, September 12. This change brings significant increases to bus service around the County and the expected reductions in ferry service for the winter months. Route 108 is now Kitsap Transit’s first frequent bus route with buses running every 15 minutes during the day on weekdays. This service change is also introducing a new pilot route, SK Ride Express, to connect McCormick Woods and McCormick Village to the Port Orchard Foot Ferry. Overall, these changes add up to 619 new bus trips every week. Beginning September 28, the three Fast Ferry routes will stop running on Saturdays.
Route 105: The first weekday trip from the Port Orchard Ferry will now leave at 5am (two minutes earlier).
Route 108: 180 new weekly trips will provide service every 15 minutes between 8:30am and 5:30pm on weekdays.
Route 109: The stops at Madrona & Red Spruce and Mitchell & Town Square will no longer be served.
Route 119: The stop at Madrona & Red Spruce will no longer be served.
Route 184: One new trip will depart Southworth Ferry Terminal at 8:33am.
Route 186: Two new trips will depart Port Orchard Ferry Dock at 11:30am and Southworth Ferry Terminal at 12pm (noon).

SK Ride Express: A new route will connect the existing SK Ride area to the Port Orchard Foot Ferry. SK Ride Express will only top at the stop at four stops: Hibiscus Cir & Yarrow, McCormick Woods Dr & Old Clifton (Flag Stop), Murrelet & Old Clifton (Flag Stop), and Port Orchard Ferry. Trips will run every 30 minutes between 5am-8pm.

Port Orchard Foot Ferry : Starting September 28, the Port Orchard Foot Ferry will lose its Saturday evening sailings. The last trip Bremerton will depart at 7:30pm and the last trip to Port Orchard will depart at 7:45pm.

Route 215: 90 new weekly trips will upgrade Route 215 from a peak only route to an all-day route with trips every 30 minutes. The route has a new stop at Olympic College. To account for the new stop, the schedule for other stops has been adjusted.
Route 219: This route will now serve two additional stop near Olympic College. Trips in both directions will have a new stop at Warren Ave & 14th Street.

Route 226: The first weekday trip from the West Bremerton Transit Center will now leave at 4:50am (five minutes earlier).
Route 331: A new stop is added at Viking Ave & Stendahl Court.
Route 332: A new stop is added at Viking Ave & Stendahl Court.

Route 390: One new trip will depart Bainbridge Island Ferry Terminal at 5:10am.

paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
